records.question: What were the specific objectives of the Tutuila Unit coral reef survey described in the INTRODUCTION?
records.ground_truth_answer: The objectives were: (i) determine the extent of coral reef development within the park; (ii) assess the general condition of these reefs; (iii) describe the coral reef communities in terms of presence and relative abundance of coral and fish species and other selected species of local/national importance (e.g., giant clams, crown-of-thorns starfish, turtles and marine mammals); and (iv) assess whether and how these reefs appear to be presently or potentially impacted by human activities.
ground_truth_chunks: The specific objectives of this survey were to:

- i) determine the extent of coral reef development within the park;
- ii) assess the general condition of these reefs:
- iii) describe the coral reef communities on these reefs, in terms of the presence and relative abundance of coral and fish species, as well as other selected species that are considered to be of local and/or national importance (e.g. giant clams, crown-of-thorns starfish, turtles and marine mammals); and
- iv) assess whether and how these reefs appear to be presently or potentially impacted by human activities.

records.question: Which coral species dominated the reef slope coral cover at Fagasa (10 m)?
records.ground_truth_answer: The reef slope coral cover at 10 m was dominated by massive corals, especially Porites cylindrica and P. rus.

records.question: How often do the management recommendations suggest repeating the coral reef health surveys?
records.ground_truth_answer: These surveys should be repeated at regular intervals, perhaps every one to three years.
ground_truth_chunks: - 1. Continue monitoring the coral reef communities in the park. These surveys should include concurrent, quantitative surveys of corals, fishes, macroinvertebrates and algae at each site. Surveys should be conducted a several depths at each site (eg. 5 m, 10 m, and 20 m), and should by done by specialist observers in each field. These surveys should be repeated at regular intervals, perhaps every one to three years, to monitor coral reef health.
